## Welcome

I am a PhD candidate in Applied Economics at Oregon State University and am on
the 2026–27 economics job market. My research examines the interactions between
private land use and natural disaster risk, and how privately rational decisions
can generate large-scale social costs and benefits. I use causal inference
methods, spatial datasets, and natural resource economic theory to understand how
disaster risk drives landowner adaptation. I then ask how this adaptation can
change future risk, generate externalities, and create a role for public policy.
My work contributes to the climate change adaptation literature, as well as the
rapidly growing wildfire literature in economics and the natural sciences.

In my job market paper, I examine how changing wildfire risk in the western
United States has affected private forest management decisions, providing the
first empirical test of long-standing economic theory. Linking confidential
plot-level forest inventory data with wildfire perimeters and fire-season
weather, I find that increasing wildfire activity and warmer, drier weather
shocks lead landowners to harvest earlier and lower their planting densities.
Using a bioeconomic Monte Carlo simulation, I find that this adaptation has
reduced forest volumes by 7–10% since the turn of the century. However,
adaptation also changed the amount of fuels on the landscape. In the 2020
wildfire season, landowner adaptation resulted in \$63–72 million in damages
from increased wildfire PM2.5 and \$28–58 million in climate benefits from
reduced CO2 emissions. Overall, adaptation created net economic damages, but a
policy requiring landowners to reduce fuels after a harvest could generate net
social benefits.

**Job market paper:** [Landowner Expectations of Wildfire Risk Have Accelerated
Harvest, Reduced Volume, and Altered Fuel Loads in Western U.S.
Forests](research.qmd) &nbsp;[PDF](papers/jmp.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [Slides](papers/jmp-slides.pdf){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm}
